title: Lab: a day in the life of a helpdesk technician
monthTitle: The Helpdesk Professional: ITIL, Ticketing & Soft Skills
summary: Bring the whole month together in a simulated shift: triage a live queue, work tickets with method and empathy, escalate cleanly, and document as you go.
objectives: Triage and prioritise a realistic mixed ticket queue under time pressure
Classify each contact as incident, request, problem, or change
Apply the six-step troubleshooting method to a live ticket
Communicate with empathy and verify identity where required
Escalate a ticket with a complete, professional handover
Document a worked ticket to a knowledge-base standard

quiz.q: You arrive to a queue of five tickets. What do you do first?
options: Triage them by priority using impact and urgency
quiz.why: Triage first: assess impact and urgency to set priorities, so the most business-critical issues get worked before lower-impact ones.

quiz.q: A ticket reads 'Whole call centre lost phones 2 minutes ago.' How should you treat it?
options: Ignore until other tickets are done
As a likely major incident: raise it and alert the right people fast
quiz.why: A core service down for many users is high impact and urgency, a probable major incident requiring you to recognise and escalate it immediately.

quiz.q: Mid-shift a user is rude and impatient. What is the professional response?
options: Lower the ticket priority as punishment
Stay calm, acknowledge the frustration, and keep helping
quiz.why: Professionalism means not taking it personally; acknowledge the feeling, keep your tone steady, and focus on resolving the issue.

quiz.q: Before closing a resolved ticket, what should you always do?
options: Verify the fix with the user and document findings and actions
quiz.why: Confirm the user agrees it is fixed, then document the symptoms, cause, actions, and outcome so the ticket is complete and reusable.

quiz.q: Describe, in order, how you would handle a brand-new ticket from first read to closure.
quiz.answer: Triage and set priority, classify it (incident/request/etc.), verify identity if needed, gather information, apply the six-step method, communicate with the user and set expectations, resolve or escalate cleanly, then verify and document before closing.
quiz.why: This sequence combines everything from the month: prioritisation, ITIL classification, methodical troubleshooting, communication, escalation, and documentation.

quiz.q: Why does a single shift draw on every topic from this month at once?
quiz.answer: Because real tickets require you to prioritise (SLA), classify (ITIL), troubleshoot (the A+ method), communicate well, escalate cleanly, and document, all together, not as separate exercises.
quiz.why: The lab shows that helpdesk skill is the integration of all these practices applied fluidly under real conditions.

body_markdown:
## The shift begins

This lab pulls the whole month together. You are starting an 09:00 shift on a busy service desk. Five tickets are already in your queue. Nothing here is new — but for the first time you must use *all* your skills at once: prioritise, classify, troubleshoot, communicate, escalate, and document. That integration *is* the job.

## Your 09:00 queue

```text
#1  INC: "Whole call centre lost their phones 2 minutes ago." (40 users)
#2  REQ: "Please install Adobe Acrobat on my laptop." (1 user)
#3  INC: "My monitor flickers occasionally." (1 user)
#4  INC: "I'm locked out and have a client call in 10 min." (1 user)
#5  INC: "Outlook won't send; error 0x800CCC0F." (1 user)
```

## Step 1: Triage the queue

Do not work in arrival order. Score each by **impact** and **urgency**:

| # | Type | Impact | Urgency | Priority |
|---|------|--------|---------|----------|
| 1 | Incident (likely **major**) | High (40) | High | **P1** |
| 4 | Incident | Low (1) | High (deadline) | **P2** |
| 5 | Incident | Low (1) | Medium | P3 |
| 2 | Service request | Low | Low | P4 |
| 3 | Incident | Low | Low | P4 |

Ticket #1 is a probable **major incident** — recognise it, raise the alarm, and get the right people on it *before* you touch anything else. You may own the comms, not the fix.

## Step 2: Work ticket #4 with method and care

The locked-out user is stressed and on a deadline — lead with empathy, then verify identity (it is an account change!), then act.

```text
You: "I can absolutely help with that, and I know the timing is
      tight. Quick security check first, per policy - can you
      confirm your employee ID and security answer? ... Thank you.
      You were locked out from failed sign-ins; I'm unlocking it
      now. Try signing in again for me. ... Working? Brilliant."
```

Notice the order: **empathy -> verify -> diagnose (lockout, not reset) -> act -> confirm with user**.

## Step 3: Escalate ticket #1 cleanly

The phone outage needs the telecoms/network team. Your handover:

```text
Ref: INC0050001 | Priority: P1 (suspected major incident)
Summary: Entire call centre (~40 users) lost desk phones at 09:02.
Impact: Customer calls failing; revenue + SLA impact now.
Tried: confirmed multiple users, network switch reachable by ping,
       no recent change noted in change calendar.
Contact: Floor lead Aisha Bello, ext. 2200.
Escalated to: Telecoms/Network on-call. Comms owner: me.
```

## Step 4: Document and close

When the Outlook ticket (#5) resolves, verify with the user, then write the record:

```text
Symptom: Outlook send failing, error 0x800CCC0F.
Cause:   Outgoing (SMTP) server setting was incorrect after profile reset.
Action:  Corrected SMTP server and port; sent test mail successfully.
Outcome: Verified with user - send/receive working. Resolved.
KB:      Linked to article "Fixing Outlook 0x800CCC0F send errors."
```

## Your task

Work the full queue above as if it were your shift. Produce: (1) your triage table with a priority for all five tickets and one line of justification each; (2) a short worked write-up of ticket #5 through the six-step method; (3) a clean escalation note for ticket #1; and (4) a closing message to the locked-out user in #4. Treat this as your portfolio piece for the month.

slides.narration: Welcome to the final lesson of the month, and it's a lab. We're going to put everything together in a simulated shift. You'll arrive to a live queue and use all your new skills at once: prioritising, classifying, troubleshooting, communicating, escalating, and documenting. Because here's the truth, that integration is the job. No real ticket asks you to use just one skill at a time. Let's start your shift.

slides.title: The shift begins
bullets: You start a 09:00 shift, queue already full.
Five tickets waiting for you.
Nothing new, but all skills at once.
Integration is the real job.
slides.narration: It's nine a.m. and you're starting your shift on a busy service desk. Five tickets are already sitting in your queue. Now, none of the individual skills here are new to you. What's new is using all of them at once, under a bit of time pressure. That's exactly what a real shift feels like, and that integration of prioritising, troubleshooting, communicating, and documenting all together, that integration is the job. So let's treat this as the real thing.

slides.title: Your 09:00 queue
bullets: A call centre lost all phones (40 users).
A request to install Acrobat (1 user).
A flickering monitor; a locked-out user.
Outlook send failing with an error code.
slides.code:
#1 Call centre phones down (40 users)
#2 Install Adobe Acrobat (1)
#3 Monitor flickers (1)
#4 Locked out, call in 10 min (1)
#5 Outlook won't send: 0x800CCC0F (1)
slides.narration: Here's your queue. Ticket one: a whole call centre, forty users, just lost their phones. Ticket two: someone wants Adobe Acrobat installed. Ticket three: a monitor that flickers occasionally. Ticket four: a user locked out with a client call in ten minutes. And ticket five: Outlook won't send, throwing an error code. Five very different contacts. Your instinct might be to start at the top and work down, but as you've learned, that's exactly the wrong move. We triage first.

slides.title: Step 1: Triage
bullets: Never work in arrival order.
Score each by impact and urgency.
#1 is a likely major incident: P1.
#4 is P2; the rest are lower.
slides.code:
#1 High impact + high urgency -> P1 (major)
#4 Low impact, high urgency  -> P2
#5 -> P3   #2 -> P4   #3 -> P4
slides.narration: Step one: triage. Never work in arrival order. Score each ticket by impact and urgency. Ticket one, forty users with a core service down, is high impact and high urgency, a probable major incident, so it's P1. Ticket four, the locked-out user, is low impact but high urgency because of the deadline, so P2. The Outlook issue is P3, and the Acrobat request and the flickering monitor are P4. In about thirty seconds you've turned a scary queue into a clear, defensible order of work.

slides.title: Spot the major incident
bullets: #1: core service down for many users.
Recognise it and raise the alarm fast.
Get the right people on it immediately.
You may own comms, not the fix.
slides.narration: Ticket one deserves special attention, because it's a probable major incident. The rule from earlier in the month kicks in: recognise it early, raise the alarm, and get the right people on it before you touch anything else. As a Tier one technician, your job here often isn't to fix the phone system yourself. It's to spot the severity, escalate it correctly, and possibly own the communications while the specialists work. Recognising a major incident fast is one of the most valuable things you can do on a desk.

slides.title: Step 2: Work #4 with care
bullets: User is stressed and on a deadline.
Lead with empathy, then verify identity.
Diagnose: it's a lockout, not a reset.
Act, then confirm with the user.
slides.code:
"I can help, and I know it's tight. Security check
first - confirm your employee ID and security
answer? ... You were locked out; unlocking now.
Try signing in. ... Working? Brilliant."
slides.narration: Now ticket four, the stressed, locked-out user. Watch the order here, because it matters. You lead with empathy to calm them, then you verify their identity, because this is an account change and the helpdesk is a social-engineering target. Only then do you diagnose, it's a lockout, not a forgotten password, so you unlock rather than reset. Then you act, and finally you confirm the fix with the user. Empathy, verify, diagnose, act, confirm. That sequence handles the human, the security, and the technical fix all at once.

slides.title: Step 3: Escalate #1 cleanly
bullets: Phone outage needs telecoms/network.
Hand over a complete picture.
Reference, impact, what you tried, contact.
State who owns comms.
slides.code:
Ref: INC0050001 | P1 (suspected major)
Impact: ~40 users, customer calls failing.
Tried: multiple users confirmed, switch pings OK.
Contact: Aisha Bello x2200. Comms owner: me.
slides.narration: Step three: escalate ticket one cleanly. The phone outage needs the telecoms and network team, so you write a complete handover. Look at what's in it: the reference and priority, the business impact, what you already confirmed and tried, a contact on the floor, and a note that you're owning communications. The receiving team can act on this instantly, without re-interviewing anyone. A clean handover like this, especially in a crisis, is the mark of a technician people trust with the big tickets.

slides.title: Step 4: Document and close
bullets: When #5 resolves, verify with the user.
Record symptom, cause, action, outcome.
Link it to a knowledge-base article.
Only then close the ticket.
slides.code:
Symptom: Outlook send fails, 0x800CCC0F.
Cause:   Wrong SMTP server after profile reset.
Action:  Fixed server/port; test mail sent.
Outcome: Verified with user. Resolved. KB linked.
slides.narration: Finally, step four: document and close. When the Outlook ticket resolves, you verify the fix with the user first, then you write the record: the symptom, the cause, the action you took, and the outcome, and you link it to a knowledge-base article so the next person solves it in seconds. Only after all that do you close the ticket. This is how every ticket should end. The fix isn't really finished until it's verified and written down. That discipline is what separates a professional from an amateur.

slides.title: Recap & your task
bullets: Triage by impact and urgency first.
Classify, troubleshoot, communicate, escalate.
Verify identity; document before closing.
The whole month, applied at once.
Task: work the full queue as your shift.
slides.narration: Let's recap the whole month in one breath. You triage by impact and urgency, classify each contact, troubleshoot with method, communicate with empathy, escalate cleanly, verify identity when needed, and document before closing. All of it, together, fluidly, that's the job. Your task: work this entire queue as if it were your shift. Produce your triage table, a six-step write-up of the Outlook ticket, a clean escalation note for the phone outage, and a closing message to the locked-out user. Make it your portfolio piece. Congratulations, you've completed Month Four. You're ready to work a service desk.
